questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and city $j$ has $(x_j,y_j)$. Which expression gives the length $d_{ij}$ of the edge joining them?
A planner builds a Euclidean network for 8 cities with given plane coordinates, where edge lengths are straight-line distances. Which pairs of cities are joined by an edge?
options: Every pair of cities, however far apart they are.
Only pairs of cities that are close to each other.
Only pairs of cities that are linked by an actual road.
Only each city and its nearest neighbouring city.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. How does $d_{ij}$ compare with $d_{ji}$?
options: $d_{ji}=-d_{ij}$, since every difference changes sign.
They are equal only when $x_i\le x_j$ and $y_i\le y_j$.
They differ unless both cities lie on the same axis.
They are equal, since $(x_i-x_j)^2=(x_j-x_i)^2$, and so for $y$.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. Two depots $i$ and $j$ are both at the point $(5,5)$. What is $d_{ij}$?
options: $1$, as two distinct cities are one step apart
$0$, as both coordinate differences are zero
Undefined, as the formula needs distinct points
No value, as no edge joins equal locations

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. A new city $k$ is added between two existing cities $i$ and $j$. What happens to the length $d_{ij}$ of their edge?
options: It shrinks to $d_{ik}+d_{kj}$ through the new city.
It is rescaled so that all lengths still sum to the same total.
Nothing; $d_{ij}$ depends only on cities $i$ and $j$.
It must be recomputed, since the new city changes the network.

questions.question: Depot $A$ at $(1,2)$ and depot $B$ at $(4,6)$ are joined by a straight-line edge in a Euclidean network, with coordinates in kilometres. How long is this edge?
On a map with a coordinate grid, town $P$ lies at $(-2,3)$ and town $Q$ at $(1,-2)$. A Euclidean network joins them by the straight segment. Which value is $d_{PQ}$, the length of that segment?
options: $\sqrt{2}$

questions.question: A Euclidean network is built for 6 cities with plane coordinates, joining every pair of cities by a straight-line edge. How many edges does the network have?

In a Euclidean network, cities $A$, $B$, $C$ have coordinates $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$ and $(4,3)$, and edges have straight-line length. What is the total length of the closed route $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A$?

In a Euclidean network, city 1 is at $(0,0)$ and cities 2, 3, 4, 5 are at $(3,3)$, $(5,0)$, $(-1,5)$ and $(-4,2)$. Edges have straight-line length. Which city is joined to city 1 by the shortest edge?
options: City 2
City 3
City 4
City 5

questions.question: A company models its depots as a Euclidean network with straight-line edge lengths, while its trucks must drive on roads. How does the straight-line length $d_{ij}$ relate to the shortest road distance between depots $i$ and $j$?
options: $d_{ij}$ equals the shortest road distance.
$d_{ij}$ is never larger than the shortest road distance.
$d_{ij}$ is never smaller than the shortest road distance.
$d_{ij}$ and the road distance are unrelated.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. To find the shortest of several edges, a planner compares the squared lengths $d_{ij}^2$ instead of $d_{ij}$. Is this valid?
options: No; the square root can reverse the order of two values.
Only when all squared lengths are perfect squares.
Yes, but the shortest edge then has the largest square.
Yes; for nonnegative numbers the root keeps the order.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. Is it ever strictly shorter to travel from city $A$ to city $C$ via a third city $B$ than along the edge $A\text{-}C$?
options: No, since $d_{AC}\le d_{AB}+d_{BC}$ for all cities.
Yes, when $B$ lies close to the segment from $A$ to $C$.
Yes, when $d_{AB}$ is smaller than $d_{AC}$.
It depends on whether the coordinates are positive.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. Cities are at $A=(0,0)$, $B=(5,12)$, $C=(1,1)$ and $D=(8,12)$, and a planner rounds every length to a whole number. Which comparison of the edges $A\text{-}B$ and $C\text{-}D$ is correct?
options: They are equally long, since both round to 13.
$A\text{-}B$ is shorter, although both round to 13.
$C\text{-}D$ is longer by about 1, as 170 exceeds 169 by 1.
$C\text{-}D$ is shorter, since 11 is less than 12.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, cities $A$, $B$, $C$ have coordinates $(0,0)$, $(3,4)$ and $(6,0)$, and entry $(i,j)$ of a distance matrix is the straight-line length between the $i$th and $j$th of these cities. Which matrix is correct?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&7&6\\7&0&7\\6&7&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&5&6\\5&0&5\\6&5&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&25&36\\25&0&25\\36&25&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&5&6\\-5&0&5\\-6&-5&0\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $A$ is at $(2,1)$ and city $B$ at $(x,5)$ with $x>2$, and edges have straight-line length. The edge $A\text{-}B$ has length 5. What is $x$?

In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. To compare two routes, a planner adds the squared edge lengths $d_{ij}^2$ along each route instead of the lengths $d_{ij}$. Is this valid?
options: No; edges 1 and 4 against one edge 4.5 already disagree.
Yes; squaring keeps the order of single edges, so also of sums.
No, unless every edge length is a whole number.
Yes, provided both routes use the same number of edges.

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. For three cities, $d_{AB}+d_{BC}=d_{AC}$ holds. What can be concluded about city $B$?
options: It is the midpoint of the segment from $A$ to $C$.
It forms a right angle with $A$ and $C$ at $B$.
It can lie anywhere; equality holds for most triples.
It lies on the straight segment from $A$ to $C$.

questions.question: Three cities with plane coordinates are joined pairwise, and edge lengths are meant to be straight-line distances. Which proposed set of the three edge lengths cannot come from any choice of coordinates?
options: 2, 2 and 4
3, 4 and 5
1, 1 and 1
2, 2 and 5

questions.question: In a Euclidean network, city $i$ has plane coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ and the edge joining cities $i$ and $j$ has the straight-line length $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$. Cities $A$ and $B$ are at $(0,4)$ and $(6,2)$. A depot $D$ is to be placed at a point $(x,0)$ on the $x$-axis with $d_{DA}=d_{DB}$. What is $x$?
